18.2.3 Physical Properties

Phenols are colourless liquids or low melting crystalline solids at room temperature and pressure.

They have a characteristic odour.

The boiling points of phenols are slightly higher than that of aliphatic alcohols of comparable molecular weights, due to the presence of stronger hydrogen bonding in phenols than in alcohols. The melting and boiling points of phenols is 41°C and 182°C respectively.

Due to stronger hydrogen bonding, phenols are more soluble in water than alcohols of comparable molecular mass.

Tidbit

Phenol and its derivatives are used as disinfectant and germicide.

18.2.4 Acidity of Phenols

Phenols are much more acidic than alcohols and water but are less acidic than carboxylic acids. This is clear from the pKa values of these compounds, given in Table 8.2.

Table 18.2 Ka and pKa Values of some Compounds

To help us understand why phenols are more acidic than alcohols, let’s compare the ionization equilibria for phenol and ethyl alcohol.

The negative charge in ethoxide ion is localized on oxygen and is stabilized only by solvation forces. While in phenoxide ion the negative charge spreads throughout the benzene ring and is thereby dispersed. This delocalization of the charge accounts for the stability of the phenoxide ion. The acidic nature of phenols, as compared to alcohols, can be attributed to the formation of stable phenoxide ions after loss of proton.

Being more acidic, phenol reacts with NaOH or KOH or sodium metal to form salt. Alcohols do not undergo reaction with NaOH and KOH but can react with sodium metal only.

18.2.5 Preparation of Phenols

Phenols can be prepared by the following methods.

18.2.5.1 From Benzenesulphonic acid

This method involves the fusion of sodium benzenesulphonate with solid sodium hydroxide at 300–350°C. The benzenesulphonic acid is prepared by sulfonation of benzene with fuming sulphuric acid (Section 16.8.5.2.3).

ایتھوآکسائیڈ آئن میں منفی چارج آکسیجن پر مقامی ہوتا ہے اور صرف سولویشن قوتوں سے پائیدار ہوتا ہے۔ جبکہ فینو آکسائیڈ آئن میں منفی چارج پورے بینزین حلقے میں پھیل کر بکھر جاتا ہے۔ چارج کی یہ غیر مقامیت فینو آکسائیڈ آئن کی پائیداری کی وجہ ہے۔ الکوحلز کے مقابلے میں فینولز کی تیزابی نوعیت پروٹان کھونے کے بعد پائیدار فینو آکسائیڈ آئن بننے سے منسوب کی جا سکتی ہے۔

زیادہ تیزابی ہونے کی وجہ سے فینول NaOH یا KOH یا سوڈیم دھات سے تعامل کر کے نمک بناتا ہے۔ الکوحلز NaOH اور KOH سے تعامل نہیں کرتے بلکہ صرف سوڈیم دھات سے تعامل کر سکتے ہیں۔

18.2.5 فینولز کی تیاری

فینولز درج ذیل طریقوں سے تیار کیے جا سکتے ہیں۔

18.2.5.1 بینزین سلفونک ایسڈ سے

اس طریقے میں سوڈیم بینزین سلفونیٹ کو 300–350°C پر ٹھوس سوڈیم ہائیڈروآکسائیڈ کے ساتھ پگھلایا جاتا ہے۔ بینزین سلفونک ایسڈ دھواں دار سلفیورک ایسڈ سے بینزین کی سلفونیشن کر کے تیار کیا جاتا ہے (حصہ 16.8.5.2.3)۔

18.2.3 Physical Properties

Phenols are colourless liquids or low melting crystalline solids at room temperature and pressure.

They have a characteristic odour.

The boiling points of phenols are slightly higher than that of aliphatic alcohols of comparable molecular weights, due to the presence of stronger hydrogen bonding in phenols than in alcohols. The melting and boiling points of phenols is 41°C and 182°C respectively.

Due to stronger hydrogen bonding, phenols are more soluble in water than alcohols of comparable molecular mass.

Tidbit

Phenol and its derivatives are used as disinfectant and germicide.

18.2.4 Acidity of Phenols

Phenols are much more acidic than alcohols and water but are less acidic than carboxylic acids. This is clear from the pKa values of these compounds, given in Table 8.2.

Table 18.2 Ka and pKa Values of some Compounds

To help us understand why phenols are more acidic than alcohols, let’s compare the ionization equilibria for phenol and ethyl alcohol.

The negative charge in ethoxide ion is localized on oxygen and is stabilized only by solvation forces. While in phenoxide ion the negative charge spreads throughout the benzene ring and is thereby dispersed. This delocalization of the charge accounts for the stability of the phenoxide ion. The acidic nature of phenols, as compared to alcohols, can be attributed to the formation of stable phenoxide ions after loss of proton.

Being more acidic, phenol reacts with NaOH or KOH or sodium metal to form salt. Alcohols do not undergo reaction with NaOH and KOH but can react with sodium metal only.

18.2.5 Preparation of Phenols

Phenols can be prepared by the following methods.

18.2.5.1 From Benzenesulphonic acid

This method involves the fusion of sodium benzenesulphonate with solid sodium hydroxide at 300–350°C. The benzenesulphonic acid is prepared by sulfonation of benzene with fuming sulphuric acid (Section 16.8.5.2.3).
